_about: Plain-English renderings for the economics and political-science shelves. Same rules as plain_english.json.
10.1257/aer.20200108: The authors built a public map of how children turned out as adults, neighbourhood by neighbourhood across the whole United States. Two tracts in the same county can differ by more than $10,000 in their children's eventual household income, and only half of that gap is explained by familiar measures like the poverty rate. About 60 percent of the difference is the neighbourhood actually causing the outcome, not sorting - which makes the map usable for deciding where to intervene and where to help families move.
10.1257/aer.20220264: Managers who are judged on their own team's results have a reason to sit on their best people. Using personnel records and surveys at a large firm, the author finds three-quarters of managers admit to doing it, it shows up in how they rate their workers, and it is worse where the incentive is stronger. Hoarded workers apply for fewer internal jobs, so their careers stall and the firm ends up with people in the wrong places.
10.1257/aer.20220831: At a large retail chain, women got higher performance ratings than men but lower ratings for 'potential' - and that gap in potential explains about half the gender promotion gap. The ratings were not merely pessimistic forecasts that turned out right: the women went on to outperform the men, including right at the promotion threshold. Two things drive it - managers protecting themselves against losing good staff, and plain stereotyping.
10.1257/aer.20231468: Standard welfare measures ask what users would pay to keep a product, which misses the cost of being the only one not on it. Running incentivised experiments with college students, the authors find TikTok and Instagram look welfare-improving by the usual measure and welfare-reducing once the pressure on non-users is counted. The result is a product-market trap: active users would prefer the platform not to exist.
10.1257/aer.20241355: Using 150 years of data across 60 countries, the authors put numbers on what war costs. A war of typical intensity knocks output in the country where it is fought down by nearly 10 percent and pushes consumer prices up by about 20 percent, with capital, productivity and equity returns all falling. The damage does not stop at the border: trading partners and neighbours take a hit too.
10.1257/aer.20240673: Who tells a policymaker about the evidence turns out to matter as much as the evidence. In a country-wide trial in Spain, two ideologically opposed think tanks, two newspapers and a neutral research institute sent identical findings about the same cheap, effective, non-ideological policy to local officials. When the messenger shared the official's politics, adoption rose by more than 65 percent; when it did not, nothing happened at all.
10.3982/ecta22451: The authors build a climate-and-economy model at very fine geographic resolution, letting people move within countries but not between them. Damages from warming turn out to be enormously uneven across the map. Three experiments follow: a modest uniform carbon tax does a lot of good; exempting the poorest countries and loading the tax onto everyone else is very inefficient; and fast green technology on its own is a poor substitute for taxing carbon.
10.3982/ecta20608: When a country won't regulate its own emitters, can other countries do it with trade policy? Taking palm oil - a major driver of deforestation - as the test case, the author finds a 50 percent domestic production tax would have cut CO2 by 7.4 gigatonnes between 1988 and 2016, and coordinated import tariffs would have got 5.4 of that, at about $15 per tonne even after compensating producer countries. Without coordination and credible commitment, tariffs do much less.
10.3982/ecta22935: Empirical Bayes methods usually assume the thing you are estimating is unrelated to how precisely you can estimate it - which is often false. The authors propose modelling that relationship directly with a flexible location-scale family, unifying several existing fixes. Applied to picking high-mobility Census tracts, the method delivers sizeable gains.
10.3982/ecta23206: Governments increasingly use trade and finance as instruments of statecraft. This paper models where that power comes from: a hegemon's ability to coordinate threats across many separate economic relationships at once, which lets it extract concessions. A sector is strategically important either because it helps assemble those threats or because squeezing it moves world prices. The hegemon adds value by enforcing agreements globally and destroys it by tilting the equilibrium its own way.
10.3982/ecta22733: Estimating how much firms mark up their prices normally requires knowing their prices - but the wide-coverage data economists actually have comes from financial statements, which don't include them. The authors show that trends over time and dispersion across firms can still be measured accurately from such data; only the average level genuinely needs price data, and they supply an estimator for that case.
10.1086/742939: Does money make people have children? Using administrative records on more than 400,000 Taiwanese lottery winners, the authors find a large win does raise fertility, though the effect is modest in size. It works mainly by prompting first births among people who had no children yet, and about a quarter of the total effect runs through winners getting married.
10.1086/740193: Using data on Finland's entire population, the authors find that people already at the top of the income distribution are much more likely to start incorporated businesses, and that their firms do better. Parental income, by contrast, predicts nothing - and the income gains from entrepreneurship are similar whatever your background, so it works as a ladder for people starting from very different places.
10.1086/739202: Using Hungarian employer-employee records linked to health data, the authors treat mild workplace accidents - ones that cause no lasting loss of ability - as a natural experiment in being off work. Even a three-to-six-month absence cut wages by 1.5 percent for up to two years, and the workers ended up at lower-paying firms. Missed chances to move somewhere better account for between 7 and 37 percent of the loss.
10.1086/740191: When Mexico introduced universal health insurance in 2002, it broke the link between having a formal job contract and having health care. Informal work among less-educated families with children rose 3.5 percent. Fitting a household job-search model, the authors find families valued the new insurance at no more than 1.33 times what it cost to provide.
10.1086/739834: The authors model social duties as things people feel bound by rather than things they calculate, separating unconditional duties from ones that depend on the stakes, and strict 'must' duties from looser 'ought' duties. The pain of breaking a duty scales with the harm caused and with how strict the duty is. The model captures behaviour that pure consequence-weighing cannot, and is tested both on how subjects act and on how observers rate what they did.
10.1086/740220: Economic theory says the interest rate should track consumption growth, and the safe rate stubbornly doesn't. The authors build a different benchmark - the return on a stock portfolio with no exposure to aggregate risk - and find it fits the theory remarkably well, and is volatile enough to explain the stock market's average return. Which flips the puzzle around: the mystery is not the equity premium but why safe rates are so low and disconnected.
10.1086/739256: Using unusually fine weekly data from a home-visiting programme for young children in rural China, the authors track how skills actually build up. Skills given the same name turn out not to sit on a common scale across levels, and each stage of the life cycle has its own learning process. Their model explains the well-known 'fadeout' of early gains as ordinary forgetting rather than as evidence the programme failed.
10.1086/740223: Economists infer what people want from what they choose - which goes wrong if buyers never saw some of the options' attributes. The authors state conditions under which choice data still identify preferences, and use the method to forecast how people respond to new information in a lab experiment and, in Expedia data, to work out which attribute was hidden from shoppers in the search results.
10.1086/739334: As children reach adolescence, parents' direct influence fades and friends' influence grows - but parents can still steer who the friends are. The authors build and estimate a model of parenting that includes this, and find something uncomfortable for policy: programmes that move children to better neighbourhoods lose their punch when scaled up, because the incumbent parents adjust in ways that work against the newcomers integrating.
10.1086/741272: An updating rule says how you should revise your beliefs on new evidence. Call it Blackwell monotone if more information never hurts you in any decision problem. Bayes's rule is; and the authors show that within a broad family of alternatives that distort Bayesian posteriors, it is the only one that strictly is.
10.1093/qje/qjag027: Tracking software engineers at a Fortune 500 firm through the 2020 office closures and the 2022-23 return-to-office mandates, the authors find that sitting near your teammates raises the feedback you get on your code by 18.3 percent and improves its quality. The gains go to younger, less experienced engineers; senior engineers actually write less code when co-located. In national data, young graduates in remotable jobs saw unemployment rise relative to older graduates after the pandemic, with no such pattern in jobs that cannot be done remotely.
10.1093/qje/qjag011: Previous estimates of what climate change costs the economy used country-level temperatures. The authors argue that is the wrong variable, because global temperature - not local - is what tracks extreme weather. Redoing the estimate that way makes the damages roughly ten times larger: 1 degree of warming cuts world GDP by over 20 percent in the long run, implying a social cost of carbon above $1,200 a tonne and making unilateral decarbonisation worthwhile for a country the size of the United States.
10.1093/qje/qjaf048: Using four years of administrative data on Chinese university students, plus random roommate assignment and two natural experiments, the authors show phone use is catching: a one standard deviation rise in roommates' app usage raises your own by 5.8 percent. And it is costly - a standard deviation more app use cuts GPA by about a third of a standard deviation and later wages by 2.3 percent.
10.1093/qje/qjag044: In a single harmonised experiment with more than 65,000 people in 60 countries, participants could redistribute real money. What drives whether they accept inequality is overwhelmingly its source rather than what redistribution costs: inequality earned by merit is tolerated 85 percent more than inequality from luck, while making redistribution 50 percent wasteful changes behaviour by only 14 percent. Meritocratic views dominate in richer Western countries; libertarian and egalitarian views are common elsewhere.
10.1093/qje/qjag028: Brazil lets private organisations run public hospitals while the state keeps the residual claim. Studying that model, the authors find it raises output and efficiency without hurting quality or equity - the extra inpatient care meets demand that was previously unmet, and population mortality falls. The gains come from management: adjusting staffing toward higher-skilled people and using flexible, performance-linked contracts.
10.1111/ajps.70079: Political actors group into coalitions around shared beliefs, and policy theory says learning between them drives change - without explaining how. The authors model a policy debate as a network evolving over time, in which actors pick up beliefs by bonding within their coalition, bridging to outsiders, and repelling away from opponents, then test the model on statement-level data.
10.1111/ajps.70070: Researchers increasingly run the same study in several places to check whether results travel, but nobody has said how to pick the places. Random sampling of sites is usually impossible and hand-picking has no statistical guarantee. The authors propose choosing sites so that the ones you left out are well approximated by a weighted blend of the ones you took - an idea borrowed from synthetic control.
10.1111/ajps.70067: Can enthusiasm for strongman rule spread from person to person? In the Norwegian Armed Forces, soldiers were randomly assigned to rooms at boot camp, so some lived among more authoritarian-friendly peers than others. Many shifted their privately reported views toward their roommates', and survey experiments confirmed that simply learning what others think changes both perception and one's own support.
10.1111/ajps.70076: Conjoint experiments let researchers estimate many causal effects at once, which is why they have spread across the social sciences. The authors re-ran the data collection and analysis for eight prominent conjoint studies, reproduced the published results, and found substantial measurement error in every one. They identify a common pattern in how that error arises and supply a straightforward correction.
10.1111/ajps.70050: Reading political texts for meaning has always meant either paying experts, which does not scale, or using statistical text methods that assume more than they should. The authors show that averaging several large language models' readings gives party positions on six issue dimensions that correlate closely with country specialists' ratings - and on coalition agreements, the model estimates fit standard theories of government formation better than hand-coding does.
10.1086/738968: Rawls seems to contradict himself: a well-ordered society has citizens sharing one conception of justice, while the ideal of public reason has them holding different ones. Rather than reading this as a change of mind between periods, the author argues Rawls deliberately offered two accounts - one for inside a well-ordered society and one for outside it - and shows the text supports it.
10.1086/740315: The author reads two late Cormac McCarthy works, The Sunset Limited and Stella Maris, as Platonic dialogues turned inside out. In each, the character arguing that the world is meaningless plays an anti-Socrates against a religious interlocutor, and the question at issue is suicide - which makes the works serious political literature about what philosophy is for and what keeps a person alive.
10.1086/741620: Tocqueville's worry about majority tyranny was not mainly about open despotism but about confusion: when everyone claims to speak for the people, how does a citizen judge what is legitimate? Working through his cases from Baltimore, Pennsylvania and the 1848 French Assembly, and then the 1854 rescue of Anthony Burns and January 6th, the article argues such judgement has to be made from inside democracy's own contested vocabulary.
10.1086/741618: The Progressive embrace of executive power is usually told as a story about the presidency. This article recovers the state-level half: the founding of the National Governors Conference, the National Association of Attorneys General and the National Association of Secretaries of State gave governors and state officials a way to coordinate across borders, build national reputations, and shape federal policy.
10.1086/739109: Kennedy thought American poetry was a democratic necessity, a counter to Soviet-sponsored art, and that the statesman and the poet shared a duty. The article makes the case by reading the seven Robert Frost poems Kennedy drew on, openly or otherwise, in his Amherst College tribute to Frost.
10.1146/annurev-polisci-032824-105816: Citizens' assemblies and other participatory bodies are supposed to tell governments something useful, but thousands of contributions have to be boiled down before anyone can act on them. This review distinguishes the kinds of information policymakers might want at different stages, the kinds of processing that turn raw input into something actionable, and who does the processing - experts, ordinary people, or algorithms.
10.1146/annurev-polisci-032624-014810: Climate politics in poorer countries is under-studied despite being where the stakes are highest. The review finds a paradox: public concern is widespread while climate literacy is low, which suggests the politics is driven by lived experience of environmental damage rather than by scientific attribution. It also argues vulnerability is not simply inherited but produced by institutions that decide who has adaptive capacity and who has a voice.
10.1146/annurev-polisci-032824-084913: As confidence in the liberal international order has wobbled, scholars have started asking what order looks like from elsewhere. This review tours the literature region by region - East and Southeast Asia, Latin America, Africa, South Asia, Eurasia - and finds a common thread: these accounts strip the liberal order of its idealised self-image and expose its hierarchy, without yet proposing a radical alternative.
10.1146/annurev-polisci-041924-012436: 'Aligned with' turns out to mean several different things. The article separates two dimensions: whether a measure captures ideological contest over the global order or disagreement about specific issues, and whether alignment is agreement (voting alike at the UN) or relationship (alliances, arms transfers). The stakes are concrete - Saudi Arabia looks aligned with China on the ideological measure and with the United States on the security one.
10.1146/annurev-polisci-042924-095655: Research on women in politics has mostly studied elite women. This review argues non-elite women face different constraints and pursue different strategies, and that conflating the two obscures what women's political inclusion actually does for accountability. It sets out a framework for the distinction and theorises how patriarchal norms, which vary across settings, shape what non-elite women can do.
